newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti looks for better times in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti looks for better times in 1997.

text.p: Italy's Olivetti will aim to put 1996 woes firmly behind it when the group reveals the details of last year's results on Tuesday and focus on its future in 1997 untroubled by its PC business, analysts said on Monday.

They expect that the focus of the results statement will be on what the information and technology group says on first quarter 1997 trading and how the new management is getting to grip with turning around the loss-making company.

Olivetti has not made a profit since 1990 and its results, to be released after the market closes on Tuesday, are set to confirm January's statement of pre-tax losses of around 800 billion lire ($473 million) with annual sales sliding around 16 percent.
"The 1996 results are likely to be largely academic, giving a breakdown of the losses, but clearly the market is looking ahead into 1997," said one industry analyst in London.

Olivetti 's late January statement put its 1996 sales at 8.27 trillion lire, but the situation deteriorated in the second half with sales off 21 percent as uncertainty over the group's future gripped the whole company.

Analysts expect 1996 net losses to range around 840 billion lire after adding some tax payments and other items, but will look for chief executive since September Roberto Colaninno to talk about 1997.
"Hopefully, he will have something optimistic to say on 1997, and clear up some of the damaging market talk surrounding problems at Telemedia and Omnitel," said a Milan-based analyst.

Market talk has focused in recent days on Olivetti's Telemedia fixed-line and media company with reports saying that it may have suffered losses of over 50 billion lire in 1996, and need a capital restructuring of its Infostrada venture.

Olivetti has denied any Infostrada financial operations -- a venture which includes Bell Atlantic and now France Telecom. It stressed the business is in a start-up phase and losses are expected, and indeed it made an operating loss of 38 billion lire in the first half of 1996.

The market also got wind of problems at Olivetti's 35.5 percent owned mobile phone consortium Omnitel and its aim to break even in 1998. But for 1996, Olivetti has said it suffered a 200 billion lire loss for its share of Omnitel's loss and this was in line with its own budget.

Some fear Olivetti's two profitable companies Olivetti Solutions, formerly Systems and Services, and office equipment maker Lexikon may have slipped into the red in the second half but both are expected to make profits in the whole of 1997.

Olivetti Personal Computers is expected to contribute a loss for 1996 before it was sold early this year to the newly-formed Piedmont International for 250-300 billion lire. The PC company made a operating loss of 10 billion in the first half of 1996.

Olivetti has largely completed its 800 billion lire of planned sales in 1996 with PCs and a 5.6 percent stake sale in Omnitel, and analysts expect the planned 400 billion lire of asset sales in 1997 to come largely from a partial float of Lexikon, while they also note Colanannio has also said a rights issue may be needed at the end of 1997. ($1=1,693 lire)
